clinical_knowledge.topic: Obstructive Jaundice (Biliary Obstruction) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Obstructive Jaundice (Biliary Obstruction) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes ordering LFTs with fractional bilirubin and an abdominal ultrasound/CT, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: yellow skin and eyes, dark urine, and pale stools for 1 week

Key HPI features: A 41-year-old male presents to the clinic with yellow skin and eyes, dark urine, and pale stools for 1 week. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Obstructive Jaundice.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Obstructive Jaundice (Biliary Obstruction).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Hepatocellular jaundice (viral or drug-induced hepatitis) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever with jaundice — raises concern for ascending cholangitis.
management_principles: Plan for Obstructive Jaundice: Order LFTs, fractional bilirubin, abdominal ultrasound/CT
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of yellow skin and eyes, dark urine, and pale stools for 1 week. HPI: biliary tract obstruction.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Obstructive Jaundice.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Obstructive Jaundice.
reference_soap.plan: Obtain liver tests with bilirubin fractionation and right-upper-quadrant ultrasound. Use MRCP or EUS when further delineation is needed. Arrange urgent ERCP for ascending cholangitis or selected confirmed obstructing lesions; involve surgery/oncology when imaging suggests malignancy.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Obstructive Jaundice
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Obstructive Jaundice
Implement evidence-based management plan: Order LFTs, fractional bilirubin, abdominal ultrasound/CT. Schedule ERCP

teaching.one_liner: Bile flow from the liver is physically blocked, usually by a stone or tumour, so bilirubin backs up into the blood, turning the skin yellow and the urine dark while stools go pale.
red_flags: Fever with jaundice — raises concern for ascending cholangitis

must_ask.say: Have your stools gone pale, and your urine turned dark, like tea?
Have you had any itching all over your skin?
Do you have any pain in your abdomen, or is the yellowing painless?
Have you had any fevers or shivering?
Have you lost any weight recently, without trying to?
Do you drink alcohol, and are you taking any recently-started medications?
